blocks.markdown: Why bank deposits are secret

In this lesson you will learn the State policy behind deposit secrecy, exactly which deposits RA 1405 covers, who is barred from looking into them, who commits the crime of disclosure, and the twist in the law's amendment history that examiners love to test. The exceptions themselves get a full lesson next — here you master the rule.

In plain terms: the government protects deposit secrecy so that people keep money in banks instead of hoarding cash at home. Banked money can be lent out for productive loans, which develops the economy. Every rule in this module serves that trust: secrecy is the default, and anyone who wants to look into a deposit must justify it under a narrow exception.

Business application: a supplier choosing between banks trusts that its operating balances stay private; a corporation keeps payroll and collection accounts in the system because officers know tellers cannot leak balances to competitors. When a question asks why the law exists, answer with the policy — encouraging deposits, discouraging hoarding, channeling funds into authorized loans — and the Supreme Court has cited exactly this intent when refusing to let the law shelter wrongdoing (as in the garnishment cases).

Read Section 2 in three parts. **Coverage:** all deposits of whatever nature with Philippine banks or banking institutions, plus government-bond investments. **Prohibition:** absolutely confidential — no examination, inquiry, or looking into by any person, government official, bureau, or office. **Four exits:** written permission of the depositor; impeachment; court order in bribery or dereliction-of-duty cases against public officials; and cases where the deposited money itself is the subject matter of the litigation. Memorize the exits as a closed list.

**Deposits covered by RA 1405** have two limbs: (1) **all deposits of whatever nature** with banks or banking institutions in the Philippines — peso savings, checking, and time deposits, and the Supreme Court has applied the law to trust and SPAN accounts (Ejercito v. Sandiganbayan); and (2) **investments in bonds** issued by the Government of the Philippines, its political subdivisions, and its instrumentalities, which the law treats as deposits for secrecy purposes.

The bar is deliberately total: **any person, government official, bureau, or office** may not examine, inquire, or look into covered deposits. That includes private snoops, police investigators, tax examiners on fishing expeditions, and even legislators — unless a Section 2 exception or a later special law applies. Three verbs, one idea: the law bans the whole spectrum from formal examination to casual looking into, so clever relabeling of the intrusion does not save it.

Section 2 states the confidentiality rule; Section 3 punishes its breach. The offender is **any official or employee of a banking institution** — directors, officers, tellers, back-office staff — and the forbidden act is disclosing **any information concerning said deposits** (existence, balances, movements, or terms) to anyone outside the Section 2 exceptions. Example: a teller who texts a client's balance to the client's business rival commits the violation; a teller who confirms the same balance to a sheriff garnishing under a final judgment does not, because garnishment is not a prohibited inquiry (China Banking Corp. v. Ortega, next lesson).

Two 'persons' concepts must not be confused. The **protected persons** are the depositors — any person, natural or juridical, whose deposits sit with banks or banking institutions in the Philippines; the statute draws no line between individuals and companies. The **bound persons** under Section 3 are bank insiders — officials and employees of the banking institution holding the deposit. Outsiders who pry (hackers, bribers, snooping officials) answer under other laws and face the Section 2 wall; insiders who leak answer under Section 3, punishable under Section 5.

Remember: Section 2 itself names only FOUR exceptions — written permission, impeachment, court order in bribery/dereliction cases, and subject matter of the litigation. Later special laws (AMLA, tax, PDIC charter, unclaimed balances) add inquiry pathways, and jurisprudence recognizes garnishment of peso deposits. All of these get full treatment in the exceptions lesson. Never invent a fifth statutory exception.

blocks.markdown: A standard repealing clause with one practical meaning: older disclosure rules give way to RA 1405's confidentiality. It does not freeze the law forever — later special laws can carve out inquiry powers, and several did. Read it as the statute asserting priority over what came before, not immunity from what comes after.

RA 1405 took effect upon approval on **September 9, 1955**. The text in force today is the original 1955 text of Sections 2 and 3, because the only amendments ever made to them — by PD 1792 in 1981 — were repealed in 1993. That history is the next block, and it is examinable.
The PD 1792 detour: amended, then repealed

In 1981, PD 1792 rewrote Sections 2 and 3 to add two examination exceptions: (1) examination in the course of a special or general bank examination, specifically authorized by the Monetary Board on reasonable ground to believe bank fraud or serious irregularity was involved; and (2) examination by an independent auditor hired by the bank for its regular audit, for audit purposes only. In 1993, RA 7653 (New Central Bank Act), Sec. 135 expressly repealed PD 1792 — restoring the original four-exception text, which is what the Supreme Court E-Library presents as current law. So when a question quotes a six-exception version of Section 2, it is quoting repealed law.

The operative sentence for this module is the last one: 'Presidential Decree No. 1792 is likewise repealed.' Everything before it repeals the old Central Bank Act and inconsistent rules; only that final sentence touches bank secrecy, and it wipes out the 1981 amendments completely. Practical consequence: there is no longer any Monetary-Board-authorized fraud examination or independent-auditor exception inside RA 1405 itself.

Trap: Supreme Court decisions decided AFTER the 1993 repeal — Union Bank v. CA (1999), Marquez v. Desierto (2001), even Ejercito (2006) — still reproduce the PD 1792-era six-item enumeration when reciting Section 2. Their holdings remain good law, but the enumeration they quote is repealed text. On an exam, always state the four-exception original text as the controlling statute, and treat later-law pathways (AMLA, tax, PDIC) as the true 'additional' exceptions.

Do trust accounts count as 'deposits'? In Ejercito v. Sandiganbayan, the Supreme Court applied RA 1405 to a bank trust account and SPAN (Special Private Account No. 858) — the fight was over which exception allowed the inquiry, not over whether the accounts were covered. The lesson: 'all deposits of whatever nature' is read broadly enough to reach trust arrangements serviced by banks. Coverage was assumed, exceptions were litigated — so argue coverage first, then hunt for an exception.

Remember: foreign currency deposits are NOT governed by RA 1405 anymore. RA 6426 originally pointed FCD secrecy to RA 1405, but PD 1246 (1977) replaced that with a stricter standalone regime — only the depositor's written permission, plus an express bar on attachment and garnishment. The third lesson of this module covers RA 6426 in full.
